s.d: a person in charge of guarding a jail or prison

s.d: a place of detention

s.c: Practically all languages have terms for a jail or a prison, though in some instances a descriptive phrase is employed, ‘a place where people are tied up’ or ‘a place to be chained.’ In some instances, highly idiomatic expressions are used, ‘a place for eating iron’ or ‘a room with rats.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:δεσμός<SDBG:δεσμός:000001>}[b] ‘to be in prison,’ {D:37.115}) a person who is under custody in prison
s.g: prisoner

s.d: one who holds complete power or authority over another
s.g: master; ruler; lord; Lord (as a title for God and for Christ)

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Have, Possess, Property, Owner

s.dp: Spacial Extensions › Extension To a Goal

s.c: Some persons have interpreted δευτεραῖος as a period of two days, so that one may translate ‘after two days we came to Puteoli.’ Though general Greek usage does not seem to substantiate this meaning for δευτεραῖος, the context of ⟦Acts 28:13|Acts 28:13⟧ may involve a span of two days.

s.d: second in a series involving either time, space, or set

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After

s.d: to take hold of something or someone, with or without force
s.g: to take hold of; to grasp; to grab
s.c: A number of languages differ radically in terms for ‘taking hold of,’ depending upon whether force is employed, whether the object is a thing or an animate being, and whether the language incorporates into a verb of ‘taking hold of’ a classification as to the objects involved, for example, long and thin, round and flat, ball-like, angular, or lumpy.

s.d: to tie objects together, or tie something around something else

s.c: ‘To imprison a person’ is often expressed in somewhat idiomatic forms, for example, ‘to be tied inside’ or ‘to be locked in the dark’ or even ‘to eat one’s food with rats.’

s.d: to compel someone to act in a particular manner
s.g: to compel; to force
s.c: In some instances ἀναγκάζω and δέω may be rendered as ‘to cause it to be necessary for.’ In other instances a simple causative seems to be the closest equivalent. For example, the last clause of ⟦Galatians 2:14|Galatians 2:14⟧ may be expressed as ‘how can you make Gentiles live like Jews,’ and in ⟦Acts 20:22|Acts 20:22⟧ one may translate ‘and now the Spirit makes me go to Jerusalem.’

s.c: There are a number of different interpretations of the implication of this statement in ⟦Matthew 16:19|Matthew 16:19⟧, and translators should carefully review this passage in various commentaries.

s.g: builder

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Political
s.d: a group of citizens assembled for socio-political activities
s.g: assembly; gathering
s.c: It is possible that in ἐκκλησία there is somewhat more focus upon the people being together as a legal assembly, while in the case of δῆμος the emphasis is merely upon a meeting of citizens. But in the NT one cannot distinguish clearly between the meanings of these two words.|ἐκκλησία and δῆμος may be rendered in some languages as ‘a meeting of the people who belonged to that place’ or ‘… who were inhabitants of that town’ or ‘… whose homes were in that town.’

s.d: pertaining to being able to be known by the public
s.g: public; open
s.c: The rendering of διακατηλέγχετο in ⟦Acts 18:28|Acts 18:28⟧ provides the verbal correspondences ‘he … refuted … in … debate.’ The term δημοσίᾳ indicates that the debates took place in public so that everyone could know or did know what was said and proven. It is, of course, possible to understand δημοσίᾳ only in the sense of ‘public setting,’ but in ⟦Acts 18:28|Acts 18:28⟧ something more than mere setting seems to be implied.

s.d: a Roman silver coin equivalent to a days wage of a common laborer
s.g: denarius
s.c: The practice of translating terms for coins with specific monetary values has differed widely in different languages at different times and in different contexts. One of the most serious problems has been the recent rapid inflation which has taken place in many parts of the world and which has thus made traditional renderings relatively meaningless or even absurd. For a number of years the silver content in an ancient denarius was equivalent to twenty cents U.S., but the value of silver has changed appreciably within recent times, and therefore any calculation based upon the value of silver content in ancient coins is misleading. Furthermore, in ancient times silver coins had proportionately far more buying power than the equivalent amount of silver would have today. Therefore, a number of translators have attempted in some measure to relate coinage to buying power, or perhaps better, to earning power. For example, in ⟦Mark 6:37|Mark 6:37⟧ the reference to ‘two hundred denarii’ is sometimes translated as ‘the equivalent of 200 days’ wages’ or even ‘eight months of a laborer’s wages.’|In ⟦Matthew 18:28|Matthew 18:28⟧ the reference to ‘a hundred denarii’ is designed primarily to indicate the contrast between the enormous sum owed by one servant in contrast with the very small amount owed by the fellow servant. In this instance the contrast may be expressed in terms of ‘thousands of denarii’ in contrast with a ‘few denarii.’ In such a case the equivalent coinage may be turned into a local currency, for example, ‘thousands of dollars’ in contrast with a ‘few dollars.’ In a number of cases translators have attempted to avoid any specific reference to a particular coin and have simply spoken of ‘silver coins’ or ‘gold coins’ without indicating particular values. Under such circumstances a marginal note is sometimes employed in order to indicate the relative value of the currency.

s.d: a marker of somewhat greater emphasis (in comparison with {L:μέν<SDBG:μέν:000001>}[b], {L:γέ<SDBG:γέ:000000>}, and {L:δή<SDBG:δή:000000>}, {D:91.6})
s.g: surely; indeed; then

s.g: by means of; through; with

s.d: a marker of the means by which one event makes another event possible{N:001}
s.g: by means of; through; by

s.d: (with the accusative) a marker of a participant who is benefited by an event or for whom an event occurs
s.g: for the sake of; for; on behalf of; for the benefit of

s.d: (with the accusative) a marker of a participant constituting the cause or reason for an event or state
s.g: because of; on account of; for this reason
s.c: In ⟦Mark 6:17|Mark 6:17⟧ Herodias clearly constituted the reason or cause for Herod putting John in prison, but there is a sense in which διὰ Ηρῳδιάδα may also indicate Herods purpose in trying to please Herodias, and therefore one may translate ‘for the sake of Herodias’ (see διά, LN 90.38).

s.d: a marker of cause or reason, with focus upon instrumentality, either of objects or events
s.g: because of; on account of; by reason of

s.dp: Spacial Extensions › Extension Along a Path
s.d: (with the genitive) extension through an area or object
s.g: through

s.dp: Spacial Extensions › Extension Along a Path
s.d: (with the genitive) an extension along a particular route
s.g: along

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Unit of Time: During, In, While, Throughout
s.d: a marker of the extent of time within a unit
s.g: during; in the course of; within; for

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Unit of Time: During, In, While, Throughout
s.d: a marker of an extent of time of the same length as another extent of time, with emphasis upon totality
s.g: throughout

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: (an idiom, literally: through years) a point of time subsequent to another point of time after an interval of some years
s.g: some years later

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: (an idiom, literally: through days) a point of time subsequent to another point of time after an interval of a few days
s.g: a few days later

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: pertaining to a relatively brief extent of time{N:003}
s.g: a little while; for a little while; a short time; brief; briefly
s.c: In some languages it may be best to translate this phrase in ⟦1 Peter 5:12|1 Peter 5:12⟧ as ‘I have written a brief letter.’

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: pertaining to a relatively brief extent of time{N:004}
s.g: a little while; for a little while; a short time; brief; briefly
s.c: In ⟦Hebrews 13:22|Hebrews 13:22⟧ the phrase διὰ βραχέων may refer to the act of sending the communication or the amount of time required to receive the communication, that is to say, to read the communication or to hear it read. For another interpretation of διὰ βραχέων in ⟦Hebrews 13:22|Hebrews 13:22⟧, see LN 59.4.

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time without Reference to Other Points of Time: Time, Occasion, Ever, Often
s.d: (an idiom, literally: through all) a number of related points of time, occurring at regular intervals
s.g: regularly; periodically

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: (an idiom, literally, through all) duration of time, either continuous or episodic, but without limits
s.g: always; constantly; continually
s.c: In some languages there may be problems involved in rendering ἀεί or διὰ παντός, since there may be a basic distinction between (a) continuous activity and (b) activity which may be defined as episodic in that it regularly recurs in related episodes. For example, in ⟦2 Corinthians 6:10|2 Corinthians 6:10⟧ the fact of being glad may be related specifically to the occasions of being saddened, while in ⟦Matthew 18:10|Matthew 18:10⟧ the focus of meaning is probably upon the continuous nature of the relation.

s.dp: Linear Movement › Pass, Cross Over, Go Through, Go Around
s.d: to move from one side to another of some geographical object (for example, body of water, chasm, valley, etc.)
s.g: to cross over; to go over

s.d: to bring a formal or informal complaint, normally to a third person, with the implication that the individual against whom the complaint is made has been guilty of doing something wrong
s.g: to accuse; to bring charges against

s.d: to state something with confidence and certainty
s.g: to state with confidence; to insist

s.d: to be able to see clearly or plainly
s.g: to see clearly; to be able to distinguish clearly

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: (a title for the Devil, literally ‘slanderer’) the principal supernatural evil being{N:001}
s.g: Devil; Satan
s.c: In a number of languages there is a well known proper name for the Devil as the chief of all demons. In other instances, however, he is given a descriptive name, for example, ‘the ruler of the evil spirits,’ ‘the chief of the demons,’ ‘the truly bad one,’ ‘the left-handed one’ (as the one who is opposed to all which is right or correct), ‘the no-good one,’ ‘the avaricious one.’ In some instances a term for the Devil may be highly idiomatic as, for example, ‘the barking one,’ a reference to the Devil’s presumed activity in animal guise.|Some translators have attempted to construct a term for Devil on the basis of the meaning of the Greek term διάβολος as ‘slanderer.’ This, however, has rarely been advisable, largely because in practically all languages there is a far more relevant way of speaking about the Devil. Other translators have attempted to render the term Devil by simply borrowing the form of the word from a dominant language, but this may also introduce complications, since one cannot always control the manner in which such a term will be understood. In one language, for example, the borrowed term ‘devil’ was identified simply as a small spirit that spreads fever among people, while in another area the borrowed term ended up meaning only a spirit which induces insanity. In this latter instance, the translators finally used an expression for the Devil which meant literally ‘the lord of all sin.’|Some translators have employed for ‘Devil’ the proper name Satan, but this is often not a satisfactory solution. In one language in West Africa, for example, the term Satan had already been borrowed but was understood in the sense of the culture hero of the people and not as a designation for the chief of demons.

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: an evil supernatural being or spirit
s.g: demon; evil spirit
s.c: While in a number of languages the Devil may be spoken of as ‘the chief of the demons,’ sometimes the demons are simply called ‘the spirits of the Devil’ or ‘the servants of the Devil.’|In a number of languages the difficulty in terminology for demons is not the absence of a term, but the abundance of different terms for different kinds of demons, each one of which may be responsible for particular kinds of human behavior, for example, insanity, depression, epilepsy, sex perversion, and violent assault. Sometimes demons are classified as ‘those of the home’ and ‘those of the forest,’ in which case the latter are normally regarded as more violent and virulent. When there is an abundance of different terms for demons and no generic term for all types of demons, one can usually select a class of demons which parallels most closely the descriptions of demon activity in the NT and use such a term with appropriate contextual qualifications so as to suggest that such a term is to be understood in a general sense.|For another interpretation of διάβολος in ⟦John 6:70|John 6:70⟧, see LN 88.124.

s.d: (derivative of διαβάλλω ‘to slander,’ not occurring in the NT) one who engages in slander
s.g: slanderer
s.c: In ⟦1 Timothy 3:11|1 Timothy 3:11⟧ it may be appropriate to render διαβόλους as ‘gossipers.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Bad, Evil, Harmful, Damaging
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:διάβολος<SDBG:διάβολος:000000>}[a] ‘Devil,’ {D:12.34}) a wicked person who has a number of characteristics typical of the Devil
s.g: a devil
s.c: In some languages it would not be possible to translate ⟦John 6:70|John 6:70⟧ literally as ‘one of you is a devil.’ The closest equivalent in such circumstances may be a simile, for example, ‘one of you is just like the Devil.’ For another interpretation of διάβολος in ⟦John 6:70|John 6:70⟧, see LN 12.37.

s.d: to provide specific information (especially with regard to some future contingency)
s.g: to notify; to give notice of

s.d: to announce extensively and publicly
s.g: to proclaim; to tell

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: to mark the passage of time
s.g: to pass; passage

s.d: to obtain accurate and thorough information about{N:001}
s.g: to learn about accurately; to get detailed information; to examine thoroughly

s.dp: Courts and Legal Procedures › Judge, Condemn, Acquit
s.d: to make a judgment on legal matters, with the implication of thorough examination
s.g: to decide a case; to arrive at a verdict after examination

s.dp: Courts and Legal Procedures › Judge, Condemn, Acquit
s.d: to make a judgment on legal matters, with the implication of thorough examination
s.g: to decide a case; to arrive at a verdict after examination

s.d: to express discontent in an emphatic way
s.g: to complain; to grumble

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sleep, Waking
s.d: to awaken completely from sleep
s.g: to become fully awake

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Behavior, Conduct
s.d: to conduct oneself, with apparent focus upon overt daily behavior{N:001}
s.g: to live; to conduct oneself; to behave; behavior; conduct

s.d: to succeed someone as the owner of a particular object or possession
s.g: to receive from; to receive in turn

s.d: a type of crown employed as a symbol of the highest ruling power in a particular area and therefore often associated with kingship
s.g: diadem crown
s.c: In the NT διάδημα occurs only in ⟦Revelation 12:3|Revelation 12:3⟧, ⟦Revelation 13:1|Revelation 13:1⟧, ⟦Revelation 19:12|Revelation 19:12⟧, and such a crown may be described as ‘symbol of his power, worn on his head.’

s.d: to give something to a series of persons
s.g: to give out; to distribute

s.d: one who succeeds another in a position or responsibility
s.g: successor

s.d: to tuck up or hold a garment firmly in place by wrapping a belt, girdle, or piece of cloth around it (compare {L:ζώνη<SDBG:ζώνη:000000>} belt; girdle; {D:6.178}){N:001}
s.g: to gird; to fasten one’s belt; to wear a narrow band of cloth around the waist; to tie around the waist

s.dp: Association › Establish or Confirm a Relation
s.d: to make a solemn agreement involving reciprocal benefits and responsibilities
s.g: to make a covenant; to covenant together; making of a covenant

s.dp: Association › Establish or Confirm a Relation
s.d: the verbal content of an agreement between two persons specifying reciprocal benefits and responsibilities
s.g: covenant; pact
s.c: In ⟦Luke 1:72|Luke 1:72⟧, ποιῆσαι ἔλεος μετὰ τῶν πατέρων ἡμῶν καὶ μνησθῆναι διαθήκης ἁγίας αὐτοῦ ‘(God said he) would show mercy to our ancestors and remember his sacred covenant with them,’ it is possible that διαθήκη denotes either the making of the covenant (LN 34.43) or the verbal formulation (LN 34.44).|In rendering the OT term brith, the Septuagint translators employed διαθήκη, literally ‘final will’ or ‘testament,’ in place of συνθήκη ‘contract,’ ‘agreement,’ since they evidently wished to emphasize the fact that the initiative for such a covenantal relationship existed with one person rather than being the result of negotiation and compromise.|In many societies, and particularly in tribal ones, a covenant is a very significant bond between persons. It may, in fact, be the most important and lasting interpersonal relationship. It is seldom entered into lightly, for in many societies a covenant binds a person for a lifetime and may even involve willingness to die for the sake of the covenantal relationship.

s.d: (derivative of {L:διατίθημι<SDBG:διατίθημι:000000>}[a] ‘to make a will,’ {D:57.123}) a legal document by which property is transferred by the deceased to an heir or heirs
s.g: will; testament

s.d: to divide and distribute to persons on the basis of certain implied distinctions or differences
s.g: to divide; to distribute; division; distribution
s.c: In ⟦1 Corinthians 12:4|1 Corinthians 12:4⟧ it is also possible to interpret διαίρεσις as meaning ‘difference’ or ‘variety’ (see LN 58.39).

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Different Kind or Class
s.d: a state of difference in the nature of objects or events, with the implication of significant variety
s.g: difference; variety
s.c: It is also possible to interpret διαίρεσις in ⟦1 Corinthians 12:4|1 Corinthians 12:4⟧ as the allotment or apportionment of such spiritual gifts (see LN 57.91).

s.d: to divide and distribute to persons on the basis of certain implied distinctions or differences
s.g: to divide; to distribute; division; distribution

s.d: to clean out or to clean off thoroughly
s.g: to clean; to clean off; to clean thoroughly; to clean out

s.d: to clean out or to clean off thoroughly
s.g: to clean; to clean off; to clean thoroughly; to clean out

s.d: to refute completely in a debate
s.g: to refute; to defeat in debate

s.d: to render assistance or help by performing certain duties, often of a humble or menial nature
s.g: to serve; to render service; to help; service; help
s.c: In some languages it is essential in communicating the concept of ‘service’ to introduce a specific reference to ‘a servant,’ for example, ‘to help as a servant’ or ‘to assist as one who must,’ and in some contexts it may be useful to employ a phrase such as ‘to help in small things’ or ‘to do the low tasks.’|In rendering ⟦Matthew 20:28|Matthew 20:28⟧ it may be necessary to be somewhat more specific about those who serve or are served, for example, ‘the Son of Man did not come in order for people to serve him but in order to serve people.’

s.dp: Help, Care For › Care For, Take Care Of
s.d: to take care of, by rendering humble service to
s.g: to take care of
s.c: In ⟦Matthew 25:44|Matthew 25:44⟧, it may be possible to render ‘and we did not take care of you’ as ‘and we did not give you whatever you needed.’

s.d: to serve food and drink to those who are eating
s.g: to serve; to wait upon

s.d: to serve God in some special way, such as a deacon
s.g: to be a deacon; to minister to
s.c: It seems quite evident that διακονέω involved a number of different functions as persons served others, especially in connection with relief to the poor. In some instances it may be best to translate διακονέω as ‘to have responsibility to help others’ or ‘to be responsible to take care of the needs of believers.’

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to serve tables) to be responsible for financial aspects of an enterprise
s.g: to handle finances
s.c: It is also possible to interpret the phrase διακονέω τραπέζαις not as an idiom but simply as ‘to wait on tables, to serve meals’ (see LN 23.26 and LN 46.13), but even so the context relates to caring for needs.

s.d: to render assistance or help by performing certain duties, often of a humble or menial nature
s.g: to serve; to render service; to help; service; help
s.c: In some languages it is essential in communicating the concept of ‘service’ to introduce a specific reference to ‘a servant,’ for example, ‘to help as a servant’ or ‘to assist as one who must,’ and in some contexts it may be useful to employ a phrase such as ‘to help in small things’ or ‘to do the low tasks.’|In rendering ‘your service’ in ⟦Revelation 2:19|Revelation 2:19⟧, it may be necessary to say ‘how you help others’ or ‘how you serve others.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:διακονέω<SDBG:διακονέω:000000>}[a] ‘to serve,’ {D:35.19}) the role or position of serving
s.g: ministry; task

s.dp: Help, Care For › Care For, Take Care Of
s.d: a procedure for taking care of the needs of people
s.g: provision for taking care of; arrangement for support
s.c: For another interpretation of διακονία in ⟦Acts 6:1|Acts 6:1⟧, see LN 57.119.

s.d: to serve food and drink to those who are eating
s.g: to serve; to wait upon

s.d: (semantic derivative of {L:διακονία<SDBG:διακονία:000000>}[a] ‘to serve,’ {D:35.19}) money given to help someone in need
s.g: contribution; help; support
s.c: For another interpretation of διακονέω in ⟦Acts 6:1|Acts 6:1⟧, see LN 35.38.

s.d: (derivative of {L:διακονέω<SDBG:διακονέω:000000>}[a] ‘to serve,’ {D:35.19}) a person who renders service
s.g: servant
s.c: In rendering θεράπων, ὑπηρέτης, and διάκονος in the sense of ‘servant,’ it is important to avoid a term which would be too specific, for example, ‘one who serves meals’ or ‘one who works around the house.’ It may, in fact, be necessary to use an expression which means essentially ‘helper.’

s.d: one who serves as a deacon, with responsibility to care for the needs of believers
s.g: deacon; one who helps the believers

s.d: cardinal number, where there are two hundred instances of a countable entity
s.g: two hundred

s.dp: Courts and Legal Procedures › Judicial Hearing, Inquiry
s.d: to give a judicial hearing in a legal matter{N:001}
s.g: to hear a case; to provide a legal hearing; to hear a case in court
s.c: In some languages the most satisfactory way of speaking about ‘a court hearing’ is to describe the relationship between the principal participants. This may sometimes be done by translating ‘for a judge to listen to an accuser and a defender.’

s.dp: Think › To Distinguish, To Evaluate, To Judge
s.d: to make a judgment on the basis of careful and detailed information{N:001}
s.g: to judge carefully; to evaluate carefully

s.dp: Think › To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
s.d: to judge something to be better than something else, and hence, to prefer
s.g: to prefer; to judge as superior; to regard as more valuable
s.c: Superiority is often expressed in terms of ‘being better,’ but in some languages it is designated by means of a phrase meaning ‘to surpass,’ so that the question in ⟦1 Corinthians 4:7|1 Corinthians 4:7⟧ may be rendered as ‘who judges that you surpass others?’

s.dp: Think › To Distinguish, To Evaluate, To Judge
s.d: to judge that there is a difference or distinction
s.g: to make a distinction; to judge that there is a difference
s.c: In some languages it may be best to render this statement in ⟦Acts 15:9|Acts 15:9⟧ as ‘he did not think that we and they are different.’

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Believe To Be True
s.d: to think that something may not be true or certain
s.g: to doubt; to be uncertain about; doubt
s.c: In a number of languages ‘doubt’ is expressed by means of idioms, for example, ‘to have two thoughts’ or ‘to think only perhaps’ or ‘to believe only a little’ or ‘to question one’s heart about.’

s.d: to dispute with someone on the basis of different judgments
s.g: to dispute; to debate about; contention; dispute

s.d: to express disapproval of what someone has done
s.g: to criticize
s.c: It is possible to interpret the meaning of διακρίνομαι in ⟦Acts 11:2|Acts 11:2⟧ as being merely adverse judgment, but since this judgment was clearly voiced, διακρίνομαι implies more than mere judgment. The direct expression of an adverse judgment may be best rendered in English as ‘to criticize.’

s.dp: Think › To Distinguish, To Evaluate, To Judge
s.d: (derivative of {L:διακρίνω<SDBG:διακρίνω:000000>}[a] ‘to evaluate carefully,’ {D:30.109}) the ability to evaluate and judge
s.g: to be able to judge; ability to make judgments; ability to decide
s.c: In rendering ⟦1 Corinthians 12:10|1 Corinthians 12:10⟧ it is essential to recognize that the process of judging must have both positive and negative aspects, so that πνευμάτων must imply gifts which are genuinely from the Spirit of God and those which are not.

s.d: to dispute with someone on the basis of different judgments
s.g: to dispute; to debate about; contention; dispute

s.d: to cause something not to happen{N:001}
s.g: to prevent; to hinder

s.d: to engage in some relatively detailed discussion of a matter
s.g: to converse; to discuss

s.d: to argue about differences of opinion
s.g: to argue; to dispute; argument

s.d: to speak in a somewhat formal setting and probably implying a more formal use of language{N:001}
s.g: to address; to make a speech

s.d: to cease from an activity which has gone on for some time
s.g: to cease; to stop; to forsake

s.d: a verbal code, whether oral or written, as a basic means of communication
s.g: language
s.c: It is possible, though perhaps not probable, that διάλεκτος in ⟦Acts 2:6|Acts 2:6⟧ may be understood not only as a language as such, but as a particular form of such a language, and hence would have a meaning of ‘manner of speaking’ or even ‘accent’ (see LN 33.102).

s.d: to be reconciled to someone
s.g: to be reconciled; to make peace with

s.d: to think or reason with thoroughness and completeness{N:001}
s.g: to think out carefully; to reason thoroughly; to consider carefully; to reason; reasoning

s.d: to engage in some relatively detailed discussion of a matter
s.g: to converse; to discuss

s.d: to think or reason with thoroughness and completeness{N:001}
s.g: to think out carefully; to reason thoroughly; to consider carefully; to reason; reasoning

s.d: the content or result of one’s thorough reasoning
s.g: what is reasoned; reasoning

s.d: to argue about differences of opinion
s.g: to argue; to dispute; argument

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Believe To Be True
s.d: to think that something may not be true or certain
s.g: to doubt; to be uncertain about; doubt
s.c: In a number of languages ‘doubt’ is expressed by means of idioms, for example, ‘to have two thoughts’ or ‘to think only perhaps’ or ‘to believe only a little’ or ‘to question one’s heart about.’

s.d: to cause a group or gathering to disperse or scatter, with possible emphasis on the distributive nature of the scattering (that is to say, each going in a different direction)
s.g: to scatter; to cause to disperse

s.d: to make a serious declaration on the basis of presumed personal knowledge{N:001}
s.g: to declare; to assert; to testify

s.d: to be emphatic in stating an opinion or desire{N:002}
s.g: to insist

s.d: to admonish or instruct with regard to some future happening or action, with the implication of personal knowledge or experience
s.g: to warn

s.d: to fight or contend with, involving severity and thoroughness
s.g: to protest strongly; to contend with

s.d: to remain in an association for a period of time
s.g: to remain; to continue

s.d: to continue in an activity or state
s.g: to continue; to remain in; to keep on

s.d: to continue to exist{N:001}
s.g: to remain; to continue; to continue to exist; to still be in existence

s.d: to distribute objects to a series of persons
s.g: to distribute; to give to each in turn; distribution

s.d: to be divided into opposing and hostile units
s.g: to be opposed to; to be against; division; opposition; hostility

s.d: to divide into separate parts{N:001}
s.g: to divide; to disunite; division; separation
s.c: For another interpretation of διαμερίζω in ⟦Acts 2:3|Acts 2:3⟧ (as middle, not passive), see LN 15.140.

s.d: to disperse, on the basis of having been divided up
s.g: to spread out; to disperse
s.c: There are, however, serious questions as to the precise meaning of διαμερίζομαι in ⟦Acts 2:3|Acts 2:3⟧; the meaning could be ‘tongues as of fire dispersing one to each person,’ but it is also possible that the individual tongues of fire were divided (see LN 63.23).

s.d: to be divided into opposing and hostile units
s.g: to be opposed to; to be against; division; opposition; hostility

s.dp: Spacial Extensions › Extension From a Source
s.d: to cause the spread or extension of something
s.g: to spread (a report)

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of διανέμομαι ‘to spread out,’ not occurring in the NT) to become known as the result of information spreading abroad
s.g: to become known; to spread

s.d: to signal to someone by means of part of the body, especially by means of the head or hands{N:001}
s.g: to gesture; to motion; to nod; to beckon
s.c: In a number of languages it is necessary to be quite specific with regard to types of gestures or motions of the head or hands and arms. For example, in ⟦John 13:24|John 13:24⟧ there is an obvious question involved, and this may require in some languages a particular signal by means of the hands or face. The same would be true in the case of ⟦Luke 1:62|Luke 1:62⟧. In ⟦Luke 1:22|Luke 1:22⟧ the gesture would have to be something which would explain or indicate Zechariah’s inability to speak, while in ⟦Luke 5:7|Luke 5:7⟧ quite another gesture would no doubt be called for, since the persons involved were at quite a distance from one another.

s.d: the content of thinking and reasoning
s.g: thought; what is thought; opinion
s.c: In a number of languages it is simply not possible to find noun-like words for thinking or reasoning and therefore it may be necessary to use a verb equivalent throughout. For example, in ⟦Luke 11:17|Luke 11:17⟧ one may translate as ‘but Jesus knew what they were thinking.’

s.d: the psychological faculty of understanding, reasoning, thinking, and deciding
s.g: mind
s.c: In some languages there is no noun such as English mind, and therefore one must use a verb expression meaning ‘to think,’ ‘to reason,’ or ‘to understand,’ depending upon the particular context. In some languages the closest equivalent of ‘mind’ may be a figurative extension of a term meaning ‘head,’ but more often than not, thinking is regarded as being in some other part of the body, for example, ‘heart’ or ‘liver.’

s.d: a particular manner or way of thinking
s.g: way of thinking; disposition; manner of thought; attitude
s.c: In a number of languages it may be necessary to render ‘way of thinking’ by a clause, for example, ‘how people think.’ In the case of ⟦1 Peter 4:1|1 Peter 4:1⟧, it may be necessary to translate ‘you too must strengthen yourselves by thinking just like Christ thought.’

s.d: the content of thinking and reasoning
s.g: thought; what is thought; opinion
s.c: In a number of languages it is simply not possible to find noun-like words for thinking or reasoning and therefore it may be necessary to use a verb equivalent throughout. For example, in ⟦Luke 11:17|Luke 11:17⟧ one may translate as ‘but Jesus knew what they were thinking.’

s.d: to cause something to be open (see also discussion at {D:79.111}){N:001}
s.g: to open; to make open

s.d: to explain something which has been previously hidden or obscure
s.g: to explain; to open up; to make evident

s.d: (idioms, literally: to open the mind, and: to open the heart) to cause someone to be willing to learn and evaluate fairly
s.g: to open someone’s mind; to cause someone to be open-minded
s.c: It is rare that one can speak literally of ‘opening the mind’ or ‘opening the heart.’ It is sometimes possible to use an expression such as ‘to cause the mind to see’ or ‘to cause the heart to know’ or ‘… to recognize.’ In some languages, however, ‘to open the mind’ or ‘to open the heart’ may refer to murderous violence.

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to open a womb) to be the first offspring of a female
s.g: to be the firstborn

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: to continue in an activity or state during the night
s.g: to spend the night

s.d: to complete an activity, normally involving movement
s.g: to complete; to finish
s.c: For another interpretation of διανύω in ⟦Acts 21:7|Acts 21:7⟧, see LN 68.18.

s.d: to continue, with the implication of movement
s.g: to continue; to proceed
s.c: For another interpretation of διανύω in ⟦Acts 21:7|Acts 21:7⟧, see LN 68.25.

s.dp: Linear Movement › Pass, Cross Over, Go Through, Go Around
s.d: to move from one side to another of some geographical object (for example, body of water, chasm, valley, etc.)
s.g: to cross over; to go over

s.d: to sail through an area from one side to the other
s.g: to sail across

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Anger, Be Indignant With
s.d: to be strongly irked or provoked at something or someone
s.g: to be irked; to be provoked; to become angry

s.d: to travel around through an area, with the implication of both extensive and thorough movement throughout an area
s.g: to travel around through; to journey all through
s.c: In order to express the meaning of διοδεύω, διαπορεύομαι, and διέρχομαι in these types of contexts, it may be necessary in some languages to say ‘he went from one town to another’ or, as in ⟦Acts 13:6|Acts 13:6⟧, ‘he travelled to all the places on the island’ or ‘… to the various towns on the island.’

s.d: to go completely through an area
s.g: to pass through; to go by

s.d: to be thoroughly perplexed
s.g: to be very perplexed; to not know what to do; to be very confused

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Earn, Gain, Do Business
s.d: to profit from engaging in commerce and trade
s.g: to earn; to profit

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Anger, Be Indignant With
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of διαπρίομαι ‘to be sawn through,’ not occurring in the NT) to be angry to the point of rage
s.g: to be furious; to be enraged

s.d: to plunder something thoroughly or completely
s.g: to plunder; to rob
s.c: In some languages one may render ‘plunder’ as ‘to carry off all that one can.’

s.d: to tear or rip in two (as of clothing){N:001}
s.g: to tear; to rip
s.c: In the NT tearing of clothing was a symbol of horror associated with sacrilege. In many cultures, however, the tearing of clothing may be associated only with insanity. It may therefore be important to add a phrase in describing ‘the tearing of clothing’ in order to mark the significance, for example, ‘to show horror’ (⟦Matthew 26:65|Matthew 26:65⟧, ⟦Acts 14:14|Acts 14:14⟧) and in the OT ‘to show mourning’ (⟦Genesis 37:34|Genesis 37:34⟧, ⟦Judges 11:35|Judges 11:35⟧).

s.d: to make an obscurity clear by a thorough explanation
s.g: to make clear; to make evident; to explain

s.d: to inform in detail and with clarity
s.g: to tell all; to relate fully

s.d: to extort money by force or threat of violence
s.g: to extort; to take money by violence

s.d: to cause a group or gathering to disperse or scatter, with possible emphasis on the distributive nature of the scattering (that is to say, each going in a different direction)
s.g: to scatter; to cause to disperse
s.c: In ⟦Matthew 25:24|Matthew 25:24⟧ it may be important to indicate clearly what was scattered. This could not be a reference to sowing, since sowing has already been mentioned in the previous statement. The reference in this verse may therefore be to chaff or to manure.

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:διασκορπίζω<SDBG:διασκορπίζω:000000>}[a] ‘to scatter,’ {D:15.136}) to spend foolishly and to no purpose
s.g: to squander; to waste

s.d: to pull or tear an object apart
s.g: to pull apart; to tear apart

s.d: to cause a group or gathering to disperse or scatter, with possible emphasis on the distributive nature of the scattering (that is to say, each going in a different direction)
s.g: to scatter; to cause to disperse

s.d: (derivative of {L:διασπείρω<SDBG:διασπείρω:000000>} ‘to scatter,’ {D:15.136}) the region or area in which persons have been scattered (particularly a reference to the nation of Israel which had been scattered throughout the ancient world)
s.g: region in which people are scattered; diaspora
s.c: For the most part, the phrase ταῖς δώδεκα φυλαῖς in ⟦James 1:1|James 1:1⟧ has been interpreted as a reference to believers in Christ. In translating, one may render the term διασπορά as ‘in all the regions where they have been scattered,’ thus rendering this expression in ⟦James 1:1|James 1:1⟧ as ‘greetings to all of God’s people in all of the regions in which they have been scattered.’

s.d: to state with force and/or authority what others must do
s.g: to order; to command
s.c: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to order’ or ‘to command’ is ‘to speak with strength’ or ‘to speak strong words’ or, in the form of direct discourse, ‘to tell others, You must …’

s.dp: Time › Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
s.d: a unit of time between specified events
s.g: interval
s.c: In a number of languages it is not necessary to have a term such as ‘interval,’ for if one says ‘after about three hours,’ the meaning of ‘interval’ is implied.

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Different Kind or Class
s.d: a clear or marked distinction
s.g: difference; distinction

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Change an Opinion Concerning Truth
s.d: to cause someone to believe something that is quite different{N:001}
s.g: to cause someone to turn away from a belief; to mislead
s.c: For another interpretation of διαστρέφω in ⟦Luke 23:2|Luke 23:2⟧, see LN 88.264.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Licentiousness, Perversion
s.d: to cause someone to depart from correct behavior and thus engage in serious wrongdoing
s.g: to lead astray; to pervert; to mislead
s.c: For another interpretation of διαστρέφω in ⟦Luke 23:2|Luke 23:2⟧, see LN 31.71. In rendering διαστρέφω as ‘to pervert,’ one should not understand the meaning in terms of ‘sexual perversion.’ In speaking of ‘perverting our people’ in ⟦Luke 23:2|Luke 23:2⟧, it would be better in most languages to translate ‘to cause our people to go astray’ or ‘to cause them to do what they certainly should not do.’

s.d: to cause a state to cease by a diversion to some other state, usually with the implication of a wrong state
s.g: to turn away from; to divert from

s.dp: Danger, Risk, Safe, Save › Cause To Be Safe, Free from Danger
s.d: to rescue completely from danger
s.g: to save; to rescue

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Health, Vigor, Strength
s.d: to cause someone to become well again after having been sick{N:002}
s.g: to heal; to cure; to make well; healing
s.c: In a number of languages there are different terms for ‘healing’ depending upon the type of sickness or illness which is involved.

s.d: (derivative of {L:διατάσσω<SDBG:διατάσσω:000000>}[a] ‘to order, to instruct,’ {D:33.325}) that which has been specifically ordered or commanded
s.g: order; command; decree; ordinance; instruction

s.d: (derivative of {L:διατάσσω<SDBG:διατάσσω:000000>}[a] ‘to order, to instruct,’ {D:33.325}) that which has been specifically ordered or commanded
s.g: order; command; decree; ordinance; instruction

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Worry, Anxiety, Distress, Peace
s.d: (similar in meaning to {L:ταράσσω<SDBG:ταράσσω:000001>}[b] ‘to cause acute distress,’ {D:25.244}, but probably somewhat more emphatic) to be mentally disturbed and thus deeply troubled
s.g: to be deeply troubled; to be very much upset

s.d: to give detailed instructions as to what must be done{N:001}
s.g: to order; to instruct; to tell; to command

s.dp: Arrange, Organize › Organize [of events and states]
s.d: to arrange matters in a particular manner
s.g: to arrange for; to plan
